schools.summary: Gill repairs the synchronism by a co-regency in Judah, supplies a second one for the length of the reign, and keeps the praise external and early.
Henry reads the reservation as a failure of perseverance and makes the comparison with David a demand for the same principle, not merely the same practice.
Clarke puts the co-regency on Israel's side of the pair and credits the solution to Calmet; Wesley keeps only Henry's clause about long usage gaining prescription.
Keil and Delitzsch take the reservation from Chronicles and explain it by the late idolatry; Ellicott prefers only, or save that, for the connecting word.

debates.question: What does the second year of Joash date from?

sides.position: The second year of Amaziah's sole rule, since he had reigned two or three years in his father's lifetime
The first year of Israel's king reigning alone, counted from the time his father associated him with himself

outliers.note: Alone in arranging the whole reign under three views, in the temple, on the bench and in the field, so that the high places stand as the measure of his religion.

themes: he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD
yet not like David his father
the high places were not taken away
the people did sacrifice on the high places
1.pericope_label: Amaziah reigned in Jerusalem; howbeit the high places were not taken away

schools.summary: Gill grounds the delay in public feeling and reads the sparing of the children as clemency with an eye to the law.
Clarke puts the danger in the conspirators' own power and the need to secure the other officers; Wesley names the virtue required, faith and courage to obey at a known hazard.
Ellicott keeps to the king's own position and the literal smote and smitten; Keil and Delitzsch set the law against the eastern custom and supply the sequel from Chronicles.

debates.question: Why was the execution of the assassins delayed?

sides.position: Until the people's affection was won and the memory of the father's crimes had worn off
Until the loyalty of the other officers was assured, the murderers themselves being powerful
No longer than it took to be firmly established and to feel his power secure

outliers.note: Alone in reading the new name as the obedience of God, given as the reward of obeying the prophet's message, where Ellicott prefers God's ward.

themes: as soon as the kingdom was confirmed in his hand
the children of the murderers he slew not
every man shall be put to death for his own sin
took Selah by war, and called it Joktheel
5.pericope_label: He slew his servants which had slain the king his father; he slew of Edom ten thousand

schools.summary: Gill grounds the challenge in the mercenaries' raid, adds an old grudge against the house of Jehu, and ends where Henry does, that pride goes before a fall.
Henry allows no cause at all and calls the man proud, presumptuous and prodigal of blood, since a personal quarrel was settled with other men's lives.
Clarke decodes every term of the fable and then defends Amaziah's quarrel as just, condemning the raid on Judah as cowardly; Wesley supplies the tone of the thistle and the cedar.
Keil and Delitzsch separate the pretext from the cause and refuse a point-by-point reading of the fable; Ellicott works the words and makes the aim the recovery of the Ten Tribes.

sides.position: Redress for the raid the dismissed mercenaries made on the cities of Judah
Nothing less than the recovery of the Ten Tribes for the house of David
Pride following the Edomite victory, the raid serving only as the outward reason

outliers.note: Alone in holding that Amaziah's quarrel was certainly just, and in charging the Israelite raid with butchering women, old men and children while the fighting men were in Edom.

themes: come, let us look one another in the face
the thistle that was in Lebanon
thine heart hath lifted thee up
why shouldest thou meddle to thy hurt
8.pericope_label: Come, let us look one another in the face; the thistle and the cedar of Lebanon

schools.summary: Gill makes the refusal to listen judicial, a hardness given over so that the idolatry might be punished, and his note on the meeting is the driest in the chapter.
Clarke keeps the captivity open, that the king plainly recovered his liberty but on terms nobody knows; Wesley takes the pedigree for a reproach.
Ellicott writes the chapter's longest note here, on the word order, the breach, the two gates and the four hundred cubits; Keil and Delitzsch read the hearse and the fifteen later years.

debates.question: How did Judah come to be beaten?

sides.position: A sudden terror, so that no stroke was struck and every man made the best of his way
A real defeat, after which the beaten army disbanded as armies usually did

outliers.note: Alone in treating the king's release as an unsolved problem, with the hostages a ransom for engagements of which nothing is known.

themes: they looked one another in the face at Bethshemesh
Judah was put to the worse
brake down the wall from the gate of Ephraim
hostages, and returned to Samaria
11.pericope_label: Judah was put to the worse before Israel; he brake down the wall of Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill fills out the formula on both sides, the might as the valiant acts of the Syrian wars and the sleeping with his fathers as no more than dying.
Henry uses the repeated funeral to survey all three deaths the section records, and judges the man void of true courage from what the annals do not contain.
Clarke deflates the formula about the fighting, since the one battle already told is the whole of it.
Keil and Delitzsch keep to the burial in Samaria and the succession.

debates.question: Why is this death notice given twice?

sides.position: Because the historian had more of the man's life and actions to set down before closing the account
Because the notice stood after the war with Amaziah in the annals the writer was copying

outliers.note: Alone in drawing from the fifteen surviving years that a man may live a great while after he has been shamed, and be thoroughly mortified without being dead.

themes: the rest of the acts of Jehoash
how he fought with Amaziah
he slept with his fathers
buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel
15.pericope_label: Jehoash slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria

schools.summary: Gill checks the fifteen years against the twenty-nine, notes the Latin reading of twenty-five, and distinguishes the annals from the canonical Chronicles.
Clarke makes the defeat and its consequences the whole cause, with the last fifteen years a series of troubles and distresses.

Ellicott argues from the unnamed conspirators to a general disaffection and reads the flight to Lachish as a sign of popular or military revolt; Keil and Delitzsch supply the hearse and the royal tomb.

sides.position: The defeat, the pillaged temple, the emptied treasury and the dismantled city, which left him unpopular for fifteen years
A general disaffection, since no individual conspirators are named, with the army possibly incensed by some particular act

outliers.note: Alone in arguing from the orderly proceeding, the royal burial and the raising of the son that the murder was no act of private blood-revenge.

themes: they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem
he fled to Lachish
they brought him on horses
buried at Jerusalem with his fathers
17.pericope_label: They made a conspiracy against him; he fled to Lachish and was slain there

schools.summary: Gill is content that Azariah and Uzziah come to much the same thing, and traces the port through its Edomite, Davidic and recovered phases.
Clarke gives the two names the same sense and places the town on the arm of the Red Sea that takes its name from it; Wesley puts the real accession twelve years later.

Keil and Delitzsch refuse to treat the two forms as a copyist's slip and read the fortifying of Elath as evidence of power; Ellicott presses the emphatic pronoun and the hint that this son was not the eldest.

debates.question: Who made the boy king, and when?

sides.position: The whole nation, immediately, the new king fortifying Elath at once
A popular or perhaps military favourite chosen over elder brothers, Thenius reading the men of war
Not for twelve years, the government resting until then in the hands of protectors

outliers.note: Alone in bringing an Assyrian parallel for a change of name at accession, Sennacherib renaming Esarhaddon on investing him with the sovereignty.

themes: all the people of Judah took Azariah
sixteen years old
he built Elath, and restored it to Judah
after that the king slept with his fathers
21.pericope_label: All the people took Azariah and made him king; he built Elath

schools.summary: Gill has the sentence of rejection pronounced later by Hosea and executed under Hoshea, and keeps the charge against the reign to the one word idolatry.
Henry takes the forty-one years at face value, answers the plea of ancient usage, and reads the prophet's commission as evidence of his own pardon.
Clarke measures the recovered territory against the kingdom's old extent and holds the prophecy of this occasion simply lost; Wesley glosses the southern border.
Keil and Delitzsch find the numbers irreconcilable and the words of the distress taken verbatim from the song of Moses; Ellicott reaches fifty-one years from a confusion of two Hebrew letters.

debates.question: How long did this king reign?

sides.position: Forty-one years, as the text says
Fifty-one, the lower figure arising from a confusion of two Hebrew letters
Fifty-one by Thenius or fifty-three by Ewald, since the son's accession will not fit forty-one

outliers.note: Alone in stating that the prophecy delivered on this occasion is not extant, since the book bearing the prophet's name deals wholly with Nineveh.

themes: he restored the coast of Israel
by the hand of his servant Jonah
the LORD saw the affliction of Israel
he said not that he would blot out the name of Israel
23.pericope_label: Jeroboam restored the coast of Israel, according to the word by Jonah

schools.summary: Gill reads the closing formula as it stands, that the acts were valiant and the exploits warlike.
Clarke explains the recovery from David's old conquests and preserves the slander against Amos; Wesley makes the reign the landmark where written prophecy begins.
Ellicott finds the clause textually out of joint and supplies the Assyrian synchronism behind the success; Keil and Delitzsch show from the numbers that the son cannot have succeeded at once.

debates.question: What does it mean that Damascus and Hamath belonged to Judah?

sides.position: That the districts were Judah's by David's conquests and were now annexed to Israel
That the text is corrupt, Judah having been written for Israel and a marginal note having crept in

outliers.note: Alone in grounding the reign's lasting success on Assyria, whose king broke Damascus while this king remained his vassal.

themes: how he recovered Damascus, and Hamath
which belonged to Judah, for Israel
Jeroboam slept with his fathers
Zachariah his son reigned in his stead
28.pericope_label: How he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Israel; Zachariah his son reigned
